wetlands.name: Chilika Lake
wetlands.description: Chilika is Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon, on India's eastern coast. Its changing connection with the Bay of Bengal creates a salinity gradient that supports fish, Irrawaddy dolphins and huge flocks of wintering waterbirds.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Water levels and salinity change with monsoon rainfall, river inflow and exchange with the Bay of Bengal.
wetlands.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; Chilika Development Authority

scenarios.label: Weak monsoon
scenarios.effect: Less freshwater reaches the lagoon, so salinity rises and freshwater-dependent plants and fish lose habitat. In the 1990s, silting of the sea mouth and changing salinity caused fish catches to collapse, and Chilika was placed on the Ramsar Montreux Record of threatened wetlands in 1993.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Convention — Chilika Lake (Montreux Record 1993, removed 2002)

scenarios.label: Normal monsoon
scenarios.effect: Monsoon rain and river inflow freshen the northern lagoon while the sea keeps the southern part brackish. This gradient is what lets the lagoon support fisheries, Irrawaddy dolphins and hundreds of thousands of wintering birds.
scenarios.source: Chilika Development Authority; Ramsar Sites Information Service

scenarios.label: Extreme monsoon
scenarios.effect: Heavy rain and river floods raise water levels, dilute the lagoon and carry extra silt. Repeated siltation is one of the long-term threats to the lagoon's depth and to its connection with the sea.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service — Chilika Lake

video.title: Chilika Diaries — a 5-minute documentary on India's largest coastal lagoon
video.note: Notice how fishing, birds and the sea mouth all depend on the same water.

wetlands.name: Sundarban Wetland
wetlands.description: The Sundarbans is the world's largest contiguous mangrove forest, formed around the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta and shared by India and Bangladesh. Tides, freshwater inflow and sediment movement strongly influence its ecology.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Tidal water moves through channels and creeks twice a day while river water and monsoon rainfall modify salinity.
wetlands.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; UNESCO World Heritage Centre

scenarios.label: Drier year
scenarios.effect: Reduced freshwater flow lets saline tidal water push further inland. Rising salinity is linked to 'top-dying' disease of the Sundari tree, the species the forest is named after.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; IUCN mangrove assessments

scenarios.label: Normal monsoon
scenarios.effect: Freshwater from rivers and monsoon rain mixes with the tides. The mangroves trap sediment and act as a living buffer that reduces the force of cyclones and storm surges on coastal villages.
scenarios.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Sundarbans

scenarios.label: Cyclone & extreme rain
scenarios.effect: Storm surges and intense rainfall, as during Cyclone Amphan in May 2020, flood low islands with saltwater, damage mangroves and ruin crops and freshwater ponds that people depend on.
scenarios.source: India Meteorological Department — Cyclone Amphan (2020)

video.title: The Sundarbans: A Forest Between River and Ocean
video.note: Watch how tides and river water shape where the mangroves grow.

wetlands.name: Tso Kar Wetland Complex
wetlands.description: Tso Kar is a high-altitude wetland complex in Ladakh, made up of the freshwater Startsapuk Tso and the saline Tso Kar. Its cold, dry environment produces an ecosystem very different from India's tropical wetlands.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Snowmelt from surrounding mountains and sparse precipitation feed the shallow marshes.

scenarios.label: Low snow year
scenarios.effect: Tso Kar receives very little rain; it depends on snowmelt. In a low-snow year the shallow marshes shrink and the nesting areas used by black-necked cranes contract.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service — Tso Kar Wetland Complex

scenarios.label: Normal meltwater
scenarios.effect: Summer meltwater feeds the two lakes and the marshes between them. The complex is one of the very few breeding grounds of the black-necked crane in India.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; Wildlife Institute of India

scenarios.label: Wetter year
scenarios.effect: More meltwater or rain deepens the marshes and expands feeding areas for migratory waterbirds that stop here on the Central Asian Flyway.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service — Tso Kar Wetland Complex

video.title: Tso Kar: The White Lake — saline lakes and Ladakh bird species
video.note: A wetland fed by snowmelt, not rain — compare it with the tropical sites.

wetlands.name: Everglades
wetlands.description: The Everglades is a large subtropical wetland in southern Florida, often called the 'river of grass'. Slow-moving freshwater, sawgrass marshes, mangroves and coastal habitats create a highly varied ecosystem.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: A strong wet season followed by a dry season drives water depth and movement across the marsh.
wetlands.source: US National Park Service; Ramsar Sites Information Service

scenarios.label: Prolonged dry season
scenarios.effect: If the dry season runs too long, the marsh cracks, peat soils dry out and oxidise, and the risk of damaging fires rises.
scenarios.source: US National Park Service — Everglades hydrology

scenarios.label: Normal wet–dry cycle
scenarios.effect: A shallow sheet of water flows slowly south. As water recedes in the dry season, fish concentrate in pools, and that is exactly when wading birds nest and feed their chicks.
scenarios.source: US National Park Service — Everglades National Park

scenarios.label: Water too high, too late
scenarios.effect: If water stays high into the nesting season, fish stay dispersed and wading birds may abandon nests. Canals and drainage altered this timing for decades; the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (2000) aims to restore natural flows.
scenarios.source: US Army Corps of Engineers — CERP; National Park Service

video.title: The Everglades River of Grass
video.note: Look for how slowly the water moves and why the timing of the dry season matters.

wetlands.name: Pantanal
wetlands.description: The Pantanal is one of the largest tropical wetlands on Earth, spanning Brazil, Bolivia and Paraguay. A yearly flood pulse creates a shifting mosaic of rivers, lakes, grasslands and forest patches.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Seasonal flooding and drying create major changes in habitat availability every year.
wetlands.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; Convention on Wetlands — Global Wetland Outlook

scenarios.label: Drought
scenarios.effect: In 2020 an extreme drought cut the annual flood and fires burned roughly a quarter to a third of the entire Pantanal, killing enormous numbers of animals.
scenarios.source: NASA Earth Observatory; Brazil's INPE fire monitoring (2020)

scenarios.label: Normal flood pulse
scenarios.effect: Each year a slow flood spreads across the plain and then recedes. This rhythm feeds fish, caimans and capybaras and supports one of the highest densities of jaguars anywhere.
scenarios.source: WWF — Pantanal; Ramsar Sites Information Service

scenarios.label: Exceptional flood
scenarios.effect: Very large floods cover more land for longer. Land animals crowd onto higher ground, while fish and waterbirds gain breeding habitat.
scenarios.source: Convention on Wetlands — Global Wetland Outlook

video.title: Brazil fires threaten the world's largest wetland
video.note: The 2020 drought: what happens when the flood pulse fails.

wetlands.name: Okavango Delta
wetlands.description: The Okavango is an inland delta in the Kalahari where seasonal floodwaters spread across channels, lagoons and floodplains and then mostly evaporate instead of reaching the sea.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Floodwater arriving from Angola months after the rains changes the size and distribution of aquatic habitats.
wetlands.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; UNESCO World Heritage Centre (inscribed 2014)

scenarios.label: Weak rains upstream
scenarios.effect: The delta's water comes from rain that falls in the Angolan highlands months earlier. A weak rainy season there means a smaller flood reaches Botswana, shrinking the lagoons that animals depend on in the dry season.
scenarios.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Okavango Delta

scenarios.label: Normal flood
scenarios.effect: The flood arrives during Botswana's dry season (around June–August), creating an oasis in the desert. Almost all the water eventually evaporates or soaks into the sand.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service — Okavango Delta System

scenarios.label: Large flood
scenarios.effect: A strong flood fills distant channels and floodplains, spreading papyrus and water lilies and letting lechwe antelope and hippos spread out across the delta.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service — Okavango Delta System

video.title: Okavango Delta Explained — Africa's water miracle
video.note: The rain falls in Angola; the flood arrives in Botswana months later.

wetlands.name: Kakadu Wetlands
wetlands.description: Kakadu contains extensive floodplains, billabongs, rivers and coastal wetlands shaped by a strong wet season and dry season.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Wet-season flooding (roughly November to April) transforms large areas of the floodplain into shallow aquatic habitat.
wetlands.source: Parks Australia; Ramsar Sites Information Service

scenarios.label: Poor wet season
scenarios.effect: A weak wet season leaves billabongs small and crowded, reducing food for magpie geese and other waterbirds and concentrating animals at a few waterholes.
scenarios.source: Parks Australia — Kakadu National Park

scenarios.label: Normal wet season
scenarios.effect: Floods spread across the plains and fill the billabongs. As the dry season returns, birds and crocodiles gather around the shrinking waterholes.
scenarios.source: Parks Australia — Kakadu National Park

scenarios.label: Extreme wet & rising seas
scenarios.effect: Very large floods combined with higher sea levels allow saltwater to push into freshwater floodplains, which can kill paperbark trees and change the vegetation.
scenarios.source: Parks Australia — Kakadu climate change strategy

video.title: Kakadu by air in the wet season (4K)
video.note: See how far the wet-season floods spread across the plains.

wetlands.name: Wadden Sea
wetlands.description: The Wadden Sea is one of the largest unbroken systems of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world. Twice a day the tide uncovers and covers the flats, which feed millions of migrating birds.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Tides expose and cover large mudflat areas twice daily.
wetlands.source: Common Wadden Sea Secretariat; UNESCO World Heritage Centre (inscribed 2009)

scenarios.label: Drier year
scenarios.effect: Here rainfall matters less than tides. The mudflats still appear and disappear twice daily, so the ecosystem is driven mainly by the sea rather than by rain.
scenarios.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Wadden Sea

scenarios.label: Normal year
scenarios.effect: The flats feed an estimated 10 to 12 million migratory birds a year travelling along the East Atlantic Flyway between the Arctic and Africa.
scenarios.source: Common Wadden Sea Secretariat

scenarios.label: Storms & rising seas
scenarios.effect: Storm surges and sea-level rise can drown mudflats faster than sediment builds them up, squeezing feeding grounds between the sea and the dikes.
scenarios.source: Common Wadden Sea Secretariat — climate change reports

video.title: Wadden Sea World Heritage Site — a unique experience
video.note: A wetland run by tides: the flats appear and vanish twice a day.

wetlands.name: Danube Delta
wetlands.description: Where the Danube meets the Black Sea it forms a delta of channels, lakes, reedbeds and marshes shaped by river sediment and water flow.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: River discharge, fed by rain and snowmelt across central Europe, changes water flow through channels and lakes.
wetlands.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service; UNESCO World Heritage Centre (inscribed 1991)

scenarios.label: Low river flow
scenarios.effect: Low snowmelt and rain across the Danube basin reduce spring floods. Lakes become cut off from the channels and reedbeds dry, affecting fish spawning.
scenarios.source: Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve Authority; Ramsar

scenarios.label: Normal spring flood
scenarios.effect: Spring floods flush the channels and lakes. The delta holds Europe's largest reedbeds and the continent's biggest breeding colonies of pelicans.
scenarios.source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Danube Delta

scenarios.label: Major flood
scenarios.effect: Very high river levels, as in 2006 and 2010, flood farmland and villages but also reconnect floodplain lakes and spread fresh sediment through the delta.
scenarios.source: International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River

video.title: Danube Delta's unique habitat under threat, say experts
video.note: How changes in river flow reach the reedbeds and pelican colonies.

wetlands.name: Kushiro Mire
wetlands.description: Kushiro Mire is Japan's largest marsh and was the country's first Ramsar Site (1980). Its peat and reedbeds support the red-crowned crane.
wetlands.waterBehaviour: Water levels respond to rainfall, snowmelt and river flow; the peat stores water like a sponge.
wetlands.source: Japan Ministry of the Environment; Ramsar Sites Information Service

scenarios.label: Dry year
scenarios.effect: Lower rainfall and snowmelt dry the peat and marsh edges, allowing alder trees to spread into open marsh — a change already observed as parts of the mire dry out.
scenarios.source: Japan Ministry of the Environment — Kushiro Shitsugen

scenarios.label: Normal year
scenarios.effect: The marsh provides year-round habitat for red-crowned cranes. Hokkaido's crane population recovered from a few dozen birds in the 1920s to well over a thousand today.
scenarios.source: Japan Ministry of the Environment; Kushiro International Wetland Centre

scenarios.label: Heavy rain
scenarios.effect: Heavy rain fills the marsh, which then slows the flow of water downstream towards Kushiro city — a direct example of a wetland's flood-regulation service.
scenarios.source: Ramsar Sites Information Service — Kushiro-shitsugen

video.title: Japan's Red-crowned Crane — the Kushiro Wetlands
video.note: A conservation success story that depends on keeping the marsh wet.

learnModules.title: What Is A Wetland?
learnModules.subtitle: The foundation

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text: A wetland is an area where water is the major environmental factor controlling the soil, vegetation and associated animal life. Wetlands can be permanent or seasonal and can occur inland or along coasts.

sections.heading: Major types
sections.text: Wetlands include marshes, swamps, lakes, rivers, floodplains, peatlands, mangroves, estuaries, lagoons, tidal flats and several human-made environments. Their appearance can therefore be completely different from one region to another.

sections.heading: Why they matter
sections.text: Wetlands provide habitat, help regulate water, retain sediments and nutrients, support biodiversity and contribute to human livelihoods. Their exact functions depend on the particular wetland.

sources: Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar) — The Importance of Wetlands
NOAA Ocean Service — What is a Wetland?

learnModules.title: Rainfall & The Water Cycle
learnModules.subtitle: Where the water comes from

sections.heading: The hydrological cycle
sections.text: Water continuously moves between the atmosphere, land, oceans and living systems. Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and groundwater movement are connected processes within this cycle.

sections.heading: Rainfall is not the whole story
sections.text: A wetland's water balance can also depend on rivers, groundwater, tides, snowmelt, evaporation and human water management. This is why two wetlands receiving similar rainfall can behave very differently.

sections.heading: Changing rainfall
sections.text: Changes in the timing, intensity or seasonal distribution of rainfall can alter water depth and the duration of flooding. These changes can affect vegetation, aquatic organisms, food availability and habitat conditions.

sources: NCERT — Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Water / Hydrological Cycle
Convention on Wetlands — Global Wetland Outlook

learnModules.title: Wetland Biodiversity
learnModules.subtitle: Life in water and mud

sections.heading: A biodiversity hotspot
sections.text: Wetlands support diverse communities of plants, fish, amphibians, reptiles, mammals, insects and birds. Migratory birds may use wetlands as feeding, resting or breeding areas.

sections.heading: Why species differ
sections.text: There is no universal wetland species list. Temperature, salinity, water depth, soil, vegetation, altitude and geography all influence which organisms can survive in a particular wetland.

sections.heading: Food webs
sections.text: Wetland food webs can connect aquatic plants, algae, insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Changes to one part of the system can therefore influence other organisms.

sources: Convention on Wetlands — Wetlands and Biodiversity
NOAA Ocean Service — What is a Wetland?

learnModules.subtitle: Ecosystem services

sections.heading: Flood regulation
sections.text: Wetlands can absorb and slow excess water during periods of heavy rainfall or flooding. The amount of protection depends on the wetland's structure, location and condition.

sections.heading: Water quality
sections.text: Wetland vegetation, soils and sediments can retain nutrients and sediments and help remove some pollutants from water.

sections.heading: Climate connections
sections.text: Different wetland types store and exchange carbon differently. Peatlands, mangroves and other wetland ecosystems are important components of the global carbon cycle.

sources: Convention on Wetlands — Wetland Ecosystem Services

learnModules.title: Wetlands & Geography
learnModules.subtitle: Why location changes everything

sections.heading: Latitude
sections.text: Latitude affects temperature, sunlight and seasonal patterns. Tropical, temperate, polar and high-altitude wetlands therefore experience different environmental conditions.

sections.heading: Relief and drainage
sections.text: Low-lying basins can collect water, while mountains can influence precipitation and runoff. River valleys and deltas can form extensive wetland systems.

sections.heading: Coasts
sections.text: Coastal wetlands are influenced by tides, waves, salinity and sediment movement. Mangroves, salt marshes, estuaries and tidal flats are examples.

sources: Convention on Wetlands — The Importance of Wetlands

learnModules.title: When Rainfall Changes
learnModules.subtitle: The central AQUA question

sections.heading: Too little water
sections.text: Reduced rainfall can lower water levels and shorten the duration of flooding. Some aquatic habitats may become smaller or temporarily disappear. The Pantanal drought and fires of 2020 are a recent example.

sections.heading: Too much water
sections.text: Very intense rainfall can rapidly increase water levels and runoff. The ecological effect depends on the wetland, its drainage and the timing of the event.

sections.heading: Timing matters
sections.text: A change in seasonal timing can matter even when the total annual rainfall does not change greatly. Organisms often depend on seasonal water availability for feeding, migration and reproduction — Everglades wading birds, for example, nest when falling water concentrates fish.

sources: Convention on Wetlands — Global Wetland Outlook

quizQuestions.question: Which process is part of the hydrological cycle?
quizQuestions.explanation: Evaporation transfers water from surfaces into the atmosphere.

quizQuestions.question: Which factor can strongly influence the species found in a wetland?
options: Only the name of the wetland
quizQuestions.explanation: Water chemistry, climate, soil, vegetation and geography all influence wetland communities.

quizQuestions.question: Which of these is a type of wetland?
quizQuestions.explanation: Marshes are one of the major wetland types.

quizQuestions.question: What can wetlands help regulate?
quizQuestions.explanation: Wetlands can absorb and slow excess water during some flooding events.

quizQuestions.question: Why aren't all wetlands home to the same animals?
quizQuestions.explanation: Climate, salinity, water depth, soil, vegetation and geography vary from wetland to wetland.

quizQuestions.question: Which process moves water from clouds to Earth's surface?
quizQuestions.explanation: Precipitation includes rain, snow and other forms of water falling from the atmosphere.

quizQuestions.question: Which wetland is driven mainly by tides rather than rainfall?
quizQuestions.explanation: The Wadden Sea is a large intertidal coastal wetland.

quizQuestions.question: What is one reason wetland vegetation is important?
options: It provides habitat and interacts with water and sediments
quizQuestions.explanation: Vegetation contributes to habitat structure and interacts with water, nutrients and sediments.

quizQuestions.question: On which continent is the Pantanal?
quizQuestions.explanation: The Pantanal is a major tropical wetland region in South America.

quizQuestions.question: Why can the timing of rainfall matter, not just the total amount?
options: Species may depend on seasonal water availability
It changes the length of a year
quizQuestions.explanation: Seasonal water availability can affect feeding, migration, breeding and habitat conditions.

quizQuestions.question: What happened in the Pantanal during the extreme drought of 2020?
options: Fires burned roughly a quarter to a third of the wetland
quizQuestions.explanation: The 2020 drought reduced the annual flood and allowed record fires to spread across the Pantanal.

quizQuestions.question: Why was Chilika Lake placed on the Ramsar Montreux Record in 1993?
options: Silting and salinity changes had damaged its fisheries
quizQuestions.explanation: Silting of the sea mouth and changing salinity caused fish catches to fall; after restoration work it was removed from the Record in 2002.
